text: Have you ever wondered what would happen if the Sun disappeared for 24 hours? A star can't just blink out, but imagine it did. For the first 8 minutes and 20 seconds, you wouldn't notice a thing, because that's how long sunlight takes to reach us. Even gravity can't outrun light, so for those 8 minutes Earth keeps circling a spot where nothing is left. Then the last light passes us, and the day simply switches off. The Moon goes dark too, and so do the planets, because they only ever reflected sunlight. But the distant stars keep shining, so noon over your city looks like midnight, stars and all. As the light runs out, the Sun's pull lets go too. Earth doesn't fall, and it doesn't stop. Like a ball whirled on a string the moment you let go, it flies straight ahead, in the direction it was already moving. Meanwhile, the planet starts losing heat. The land, the air and the oceans give back the warmth they soaked up, like the bricks of a fireplace after the fire goes out. So the dark day feels like one very long winter night: cold, but not frozen. For plants, though, a clock starts ticking. Photosynthesis stops, and nearly all life on the surface, including us, depends on it. Then, after 24 hours, the Sun comes back. When its light arrives, again 8 minutes later, there's no sunrise: over your city at noon, the Sun just switches on in the middle of the sky. Its gravity comes with that light and catches Earth in a slightly different orbit. And that delay never goes away: even on an ordinary day, the sunlight on your face left the Sun 8 minutes ago. We've always lived a few minutes behind our star.
